evidence.quote: The road descends a canyon filled with yellow- and gray-striped hills.

evidence.claim: The route belongs to New Mexico’s designated scenic byways.

evidence.claim: At Chaco, roads linked the canyon with outlying communities.

evidence.quote: The Salmon Ruins pueblo and museum are located just to the west of the city along Highway 64.

evidence.claim: Westward from the Farmington area, US 64 leads toward the striped canyon country and Arizona.

evidence.claim: At Pueblo Bonito, sandstone masonry walls reached three feet thick to carry multistory construction.
evidence.quote: The builders' use of core-and-veneer architecture and multi-story construction necessitated massive masonry walls up to 3 ft (91 cm) thick.

evidence.claim: Parts of the complex rose four stories, and it contains at least 650 rooms.
evidence.quote: comprising at least 650 rooms, it is the largest great house; in parts of the complex, the structure was four stories high.

evidence.claim: Chacoans quarried stone and brought timber from distant sources to build the canyon’s major complexes.
evidence.quote: Chacoans quarried sandstone blocks and hauled timber from great distances, assembling 15 major complexes

evidence.claim: The walls combined parallel stone faces with rubble cores and veneers of smaller sandstone pieces.
evidence.quote: Gaps between walls were packed with rubble, forming the wall's core. Walls were then covered in a veneer of small sandstone pieces

evidence.claim: Hopi and Pueblo peoples consider these sites sacred ancestral homelands and maintain oral accounts of their relationship to Chaco.
evidence.quote: The sites are considered sacred ancestral homelands by the Hopi and Pueblo peoples, who maintain oral accounts of their historical migration from Chaco and their spiritual relationship to the land.

evidence.claim: The name records a mistake: 19th-century American settlers attributed these Puebloan buildings to the Aztecs of central Mexico.
evidence.quote: The Puebloan-built ruins were dubbed the "Aztec Ruins" by 19th- century American settlers, who misattributed their construction to the Aztecs, an indigenous people historically based in central Mexico.

evidence.claim: The preserved structures stand on the western bank of the Animas River.
evidence.quote: The national monument lies on the western bank of the Animas River

evidence.claim: Archaeological evidence dates construction to the 12th and 13th centuries.
evidence.quote: Archaeological evidence puts the construction of the ruins in the 12th and 13th centuries.

evidence.claim: The site became a national monument in 1923 and was included in the Chaco Culture World Heritage designation in 1987.
evidence.quote: The site was declared "Aztec Ruin National Monument" on January 24, 1923.

evidence.claim: Within the monument, the Hubbard Site’s tri-wall structure resembles a building at Pueblo del Arroyo in Chaco Canyon.

evidence.quote: (UNESCO) listed the Chaco Culture as a World Heritage Site on December 8, 1987. That listing specifically included the Aztec Ruins.

flags: The cache does not document the modern byway’s builders, campaign or designation date. The history paragraph instead explains earlier travel routes and site protection, without claiming continuity of road alignment.

Material describes a road network and resets strip mileages at Crownpoint. Moments are ordered El Morro (Ramah–Grants section), Chaco (before Bloomfield), then Aztec north of Bloomfield; this is a regional sequence, not turn-by-turn navigation.

Tourism dates both northern outliers to the eleventh century; the Aztec article dates its structures to the twelfth and thirteenth. Dropped the current blanket eleventh-century claim and used the site-specific chronology.
The cache supports the current Chaco largest-buildings claim but supplies no underlying architectural comparison; omitted the superlative for precision.
Dropped the ocean-liner simile and unqualified lonely-road language, which were tourism rhetoric rather than observations.
FHWA lists a multistate national byway but does not delimit its New Mexico segments. No national status is assigned to this entire catalog network.

No park-manager road-condition page is cached; no current access-road condition, schedule or drive time is asserted. Tribal cultural statements rely on secondary evidence because no community-authored page is available.
